scope: Only the three priority launch videos, per direct user reply.
editorial_status: Detailed creative proposals; confirmed user decisions are separated inside each episode.
intelligence_access: Public Influint exports refreshed October 15. Gaming premise/escalation/rules and swap-test guidance remain Theory, not measured guarantees.
measurement: Use actual 24-hour, 7-day and first-28-day results per upload. No private CTR or retention curves are available.

episodes.title: I Beat The World’s Best Video Game
episodes.summary: Five cast members each enter a different game crossover, complete a clear personal challenge and reunite to defeat one shared Godzilla.
episodes.status: Launch direction confirmed; the five pairings, cast assignments and mechanics below are a creative proposal.
episodes.viewer_promise: Five impossible experiences become one game the crew must beat together. The appeal is discovery, competitive reactions and a giant shared payoff; viewers need no prior game knowledge.
confirmed: Alex, Alan, Kat, Tanner and Shawn each have their own setup and one different crossover.
Intercut the five experiences; nobody is required to tour all five worlds.
All five join one final Godzilla fight.
Lead packaging with I Beat The World’s Best Video Game; the other existing titles remain tests.
episodes.objective: Clear one simple mission in each world, then survive and defeat Godzilla as a team.

rules.label: Start
rules.text: Introduce the five players and their five different missions before the first meaningful attempt. Use one face/name/world marker per person.

rules.label: Individual success
rules.text: Every mission has one visible finish condition. Each player earns a team ability for the finale by clearing their own mission; the abilities below are proposals to test.

rules.label: Failure and help
rules.text: A failed attempt returns to a disclosed checkpoint with a visible consequence. Players can exchange advice; they stay in their own worlds. No surprise eliminations.

rules.label: Convergence
rules.text: Once all five missions are cleared, move all players to the tested common arena. Show this transition clearly; seamless networking between different game engines is not required.

rules.label: Final win
rules.text: Destroy the three visible boss weak points, then complete the final team attack. If the team wipes, show the failed attempt and retry under the same disclosed rules.

intro.label: 0 (First Frame)–5s
intro.text: A real host rides a dragon over an impossible game collision, or another equally clear playable hero moment. Smash-cut to Godzilla towering over the crew. This shot only leads if its gameplay has been proved.

intro.label: 5s–15s
intro.text: “We combined our favorite games, gave everyone a different world, and now we have to beat them all.” Show five quick player/world reveals with one plain-language goal each.

intro.label: 15s–30s
intro.text: Start one real attempt: a car approaches a missing block bridge, then cut to a completely different player discovering their own problem. Leave the first outcome open only until the next relevant return.

worlds.name: Build the getaway
worlds.goal: Deliver one marked car across a broken block-built route to a rescue pad.
worlds.mechanic: Three road gaps require a choice between limited bridge pieces, a risky ramp or a longer route. Building changes the driving problem.
worlds.failure: Falling or losing the marked car resets to the previous checkpoint and consumes the disclosed retry consequence.
worlds.escalation: The last bridge must support the car while pursuing enemies close in.
worlds.finale_role: Proposed: build a short bridge or shield platform so the team can reach a boss weak point.
worlds.proof: One drive/build/reset loop in a bounded GTA 5/custom scene. Cosmetic blocks alone do not deliver this crossover.
worlds.fallback: Use a small tested block course with prebuilt placement choices instead of free building across a whole city.

worlds.pairing: Minecraft × Halo, with optional Call of Duty-style horde detail
worlds.name: Dragon rescue
worlds.goal: Disable three visible invasion beacons and rescue the villagers below.
worlds.mechanic: Ride a dragon and use a tested ranged weapon against beacon guards; Halo/Flood-inspired threats give the familiar Minecraft setting a new problem.
worlds.failure: Losing the dragon or a failed beacon approach returns to a clear checkpoint. Keep the rescue target count visible.
worlds.escalation: The final beacon is protected by a larger wave, forcing a low pass or a different attack angle.
worlds.finale_role: Proposed: aerial distraction and an attack on the high weak point.
worlds.proof: Rider control, aiming, target damage and reset must work together. The existing dragon and Halo component listings do not prove compatibility.
worlds.fallback: A short controllable dragon segment followed by a ground defense; revise the thumbnail if mounted weapon use is not playable.

worlds.name: Tiny companion, giant enemy
worlds.goal: Recruit one small companion and use its ability to defeat a much larger guardian.
worlds.mechanic: Choose between two readable companion abilities, then learn a visible boss attack and exploit its opening. Explain “catch a helper, dodge the giant, hit the weak spot.”
worlds.failure: A missed capture or boss defeat triggers the same agreed retry; no hidden stat or lore requirement.
worlds.escalation: The guardian changes its attack in phase two, making the first strategy insufficient.
worlds.finale_role: Proposed: a support ability that protects or revives one teammate during the shared fight.
worlds.proof: One bounded capture/companion/boss interaction in an approved custom route. Do not assume the commercial games can be networked together.
worlds.fallback: One fixed companion with one support action and a single custom guardian arena.

worlds.name: The impossible delivery
worlds.goal: Carry a marked package through three city checkpoints and cross the finish with it.
worlds.mechanic: Kart-style items change a GTA-style road race: a boost opens a route, a shell forces a dodge, and a shortcut trades speed for danger.
worlds.failure: Dropping the package or missing a checkpoint returns to the last checkpoint; shortcuts count only inside the marked route.
worlds.escalation: A giant chasing obstacle interrupts the final straight, making the item choice matter.
worlds.finale_role: Proposed: drive a distraction vehicle to pull Godzilla away from the ground team.
worlds.proof: A short race course with working items, route checks and reliable resets. Equalize the tested controls before recording.
worlds.fallback: Two reliable items and three designed corners, rather than an entire new racing system.

worlds.name: Build before nightfall
worlds.goal: Protect one rescue beacon through three increasingly difficult night waves.
worlds.mechanic: Gather a small material allowance and build defenses before a shrinking safe area and a visible creature wave reach the beacon.
worlds.failure: Beacon destruction resets the wave with the disclosed consequence; do not turn it into an unexplained survival grind.
worlds.escalation: The last wave attacks from two sides, forcing a tradeoff between repairing defenses and fighting.
worlds.finale_role: Proposed: place a defensive shelter or temporary cover during Godzilla’s area attack.
worlds.proof: One build/defend/wave loop in a bounded custom scene. Roblox/Fortnite integration is a creative direction, not a confirmed cross-platform mod.
worlds.fallback: Fixed defensive placement points and three short waves with a clear safe-zone boundary.

story.action: Give each cast member an immediately different problem. Start with the clearest collision, then introduce the others through action rather than five long explanations.
story.question: Which world would you choose, and who has the hardest mission?

story.action: Cut between meaningful discoveries: one player finds a shortcut, another wastes a scarce tool, another learns a boss pattern. Return before an open question feels abandoned.
story.question: Can the crew turn these unfamiliar mechanics to their advantage?

story.action: Reveal the next obstacle when a player appears comfortable. Use visible progress and honest resets; do not manufacture the same setback for everyone.
story.question: Will the last unfinished mission hold everyone back?

story.action: Show every mission’s actual finish and the ability it contributes. A simple transition moves the cast into one common arena.
story.question: Will five very different abilities work together?

story.action: Phase one teaches a readable attack. Phase two requires two roles to cooperate. The final weak point needs the full team’s coordinated attempt.
story.question: Can they complete the team attack before the boss overwhelms them?

story.action: Show the actual winning hit, immediate cast reactions and a concise look back at the five worlds. If the filmed result changes, let the result determine the ending.
story.question: Did this custom game earn the “world’s best” claim for this crew?

finale.label: Readable objective
finale.text: One Godzilla, one arena and three visible weak points. Keep the boss and team progress on screen; avoid five separate meters viewers cannot interpret.

finale.label: Meaningful cooperation
finale.text: Ground distraction exposes a target, a builder creates access, the flyer reaches the high point, and support/defense keeps the attempt alive. Roles can be swapped after testing for actual fun and balance.

finale.label: Earned jeopardy
finale.text: Telegraph a stomp or area attack so viewers understand why the crew moves. A failed coordinated attack creates a real recovery problem rather than an arbitrary cutscene.

finale.label: Actual team gameplay
finale.text: The five players must affect the shared fight. Cinematic inserts can show scale; a rendered sequence cannot stand in for their participation.

cast_roles.label: Proposed assignment
cast_roles.text: Alex: build/getaway; Alan: aerial rescue; Kat: companion/boss; Tanner: item race; Shawn: build/defend. Reassign from playtests and cast preference; these are not approved assignments.

cast_roles.label: Ensemble edit
cast_roles.text: Rotate discovery, competence, mistakes and recoveries across the entire cast. Neither twin automatically owns every important beat.

hero_moments.label: A collision that changes the action
hero_moments.text: A block bridge changes a car route; a tiny companion counters a giant; a familiar kart item becomes a city-scale problem. Show the mechanic causing the result.

hero_moments.label: The last solo finish
hero_moments.text: The others can advise and react while the last player attempts their mission. Keep the outcome genuine and include the successful attempt.

hero_moments.label: Five-player rescue
hero_moments.text: One player’s mistake during the boss fight creates a clear reason for another player’s earned ability to matter.

packaging.label: Representative collision
packaging.text: Photographic Stokes host on the playable dragon with one clean threat group below, luminous blue sky and minimal text. Retain as a reference until the flight/weapon mechanic is proved.

packaging.label: Five worlds, one threat
packaging.text: One large human foreground, a simple five-region world composition and a dominant Godzilla silhouette. Distinct worlds must read as regions, not a logo collage.

packaging.label: Team versus the boss
packaging.text: Real cast foreground reacting to an enormous Godzilla in a game arena. Keep one face dominant and the other players supportive so the image works at phone size.

production.label: Minimum playable proof
production.text: Prove one individual mission, the common five-client arena and the handoff before expanding the other worlds. Record an actual control-to-outcome test.

production.label: Repeatable recovery
production.text: Every scene needs a known reset, a working save/checkpoint and a way to restore a failed client without pretending the failure did not happen.

production.label: Capture needs
production.text: Save each individual game feed and player reaction separately, plus the common finale feeds. Preserve the moment that proves each mission and the final win.

production.label: Scope boundary
production.text: Modded GTA 5 and a separate recreation with AI-assisted development are candidates. A wholly new engine or seamless engine-to-engine networking is not assumed complete.

post.label: Comprehension
post.text: Use a consistent cast/name/world marker, one sentence of rules at first use and a visible objective. Explain the consequence of an item before relying on game knowledge.

post.label: Intercutting
post.text: Cut when a discovery, decision or consequence earns the next point of view. Do not alternate mechanically just to give everyone equal seconds.

post.label: Finale transition
post.text: Explain that the five experiences lead into the common boss arena; use the same earned ability labels so the transition feels like a payoff.

post.label: Localization
post.text: Prefer icons, simple verbs and short labels. Keep jokes understandable through action and reactions; separate dialogue, music and game sound for later localization.

shorts.label: Impossible interaction
shorts.text: One recognizable crossover, a first attempt and its result in a self-contained extract.

shorts.label: Crew recovery
shorts.text: A player makes a readable mistake, then a teammate’s advice or ability changes the outcome.

shorts.label: Shared boss payoff
shorts.text: A short role/reversal/winning action that makes sense without explaining all five worlds.

success_checks: A new viewer can name each player’s goal after its first reveal.
The package depicts a mechanic or scene that actually exists in the finished episode.
Every world contributes a distinctive discovery and a visible result.
The shared boss resolves the five-world story instead of feeling like an unrelated extra video.
open_choices: Approve or revise the five proposed pairings and cast assignments.
Choose the exact mission finish conditions, retry consequences and finale abilities after prototype playtests.
Select a title/composition matched to the proved hero moment; commission revised artwork only after that choice.

references.title: World's Largest Minecraft Build!
references.use: Observed thumbnail: large real host beside a block-built Earth with bright blue sky. Style/composition reference only; no claim this validates the new crossover.

references.title: Halo & MDE
references.use: Developer-maintained Halo mod listing. Candidate component, not a tested full crossover stack.

references.title: Dragon Mounts Remastered
references.use: Developer-maintained rideable dragon mod listing. Does not establish that the exact Ender Dragon and gun combination works.

references.title: Immersive Vehicles
references.use: Developer-maintained vehicle framework. Candidate tool, not evidence of GTA integration.

episodes.evidence_note: Existing composition and component references are adjacent evidence. They do not establish a working nine-game stack, tested five-world retention or causal thumbnail lift.

episodes.title: I Found The Leaked GTA 6
episodes.summary: Alex gives the crew a convincing custom “early GTA 6” experience, lets their suspicions build and reveals how he fooled them.
episodes.status: Alex’s prank and audience uncertainty are confirmed; the mission sequence and reveal mechanics below are proposed.
episodes.viewer_promise: An extraordinary-looking game raises one question: is this actually real? The audience gets enough clues to form a theory while the cast tries to finish a fun challenge.
confirmed: Alex is the informed prankster; Alan, Kat, Tanner and Shawn are the intended targets.
Keep the audience guessing from the opening rather than announcing the prank immediately.
The experience is a staged GTA 5/custom build, not a genuine GTA 6 leak.
Confirm actual briefing history before describing a reaction as unaware.
episodes.objective: The crew attempts three increasingly strange missions while Alex tries to keep his supposed early build believable until the final reveal.

rules.label: Player objective
rules.text: Deliver one marked car, complete a short escape and reach a final reveal location. The cast can understand the task even if they have never played GTA.

rules.label: Alex’s constraint
rules.text: He operates only the prepared changes. He must answer the crew’s challenges using the actual build; he cannot simply declare every impossible event normal.

rules.label: Suspicion
rules.text: Track real questions and predictions in the edit. A suspicion board is an editorial device, not a score that guarantees everyone is fooled.

rules.label: Retries
rules.text: Technical crashes are production failures, not proof of an intentional prank. Use a tested restart point and be truthful if a failure affects the story.

rules.label: Payoff
rules.text: The final location exposes the mechanism and Alex takes responsibility. Show the crew understanding the trick and trying the revealed mechanic themselves.

intro.label: 0 (First Frame)–5s
intro.text: Show a convincing-looking sunny city/game moment and a genuine “how did you get this?” reaction. Avoid an opening explanation that gives away the trick.

intro.label: 5s–15s
intro.text: Alex presents the supposed access and the crew starts one simple mission. Establish what would make the experience extraordinary without inventing a real leaked source.

intro.label: 15s–30s
intro.text: A small unusual detail creates the first doubt, but a playable driving moment pulls the crew back into the challenge. Let the audience start forming its own theory.

story.action: A convincing single district, responsive car handling and one polished interaction establish why the crew would keep playing. Use only apparent proof the staged premise can support.
story.question: Did Alex really get something nobody else has?

story.action: The crew follows an easy route to a marked destination. A subtle repeated character, oddly familiar building or unusual sign gives attentive viewers a clue.
story.question: Is that detail a clue or just an unfinished game?

story.action: A controlled chase introduces one absurd behavior that is still playable. The crew tests Alex’s explanation instead of passively listening to it.
story.question: Can the build survive an unscripted test?

story.action: Let a real suspicion change the action: take an unexpected turn, revisit the odd interaction or ask to try a different vehicle. Preserve the cause-and-effect chain.
story.question: Who will work out what Alex changed?

story.action: The final objective leads to a location that exposes the setup: a custom room or world element directly tied to Alex and the crew. It should answer earlier clues.
story.question: What is behind the final door?

story.action: Alex explains the custom GTA 5/recreation route in plain language. Show brief proof of the trick and the crew’s real responses, then give them a short turn playing with it knowingly.
story.question: Which clue should have given it away?

cast_roles.label: Alex
cast_roles.text: Owns the misdirection, responds to suspicion and delivers the reveal. His control is the story’s engine, but the edit can withhold selected information until payoff.

cast_roles.label: Alan, Kat, Tanner and Shawn
cast_roles.text: Each gets a distinct attempt or investigation: driving, testing an interaction, following a clue or challenging Alex’s explanation. Assign the exact missions around authentic reactions, not predetermined “believer” or “skeptic” roles.

cast_roles.label: Knowledge boundary
cast_roles.text: Separate people who know the setup from the intended targets before filming. If someone already knows, use their actual role rather than presenting them as fooled.

hero_moments.label: Almost caught
hero_moments.text: A target tests something Alex did not expect. Hold enough of the interaction to show whether his explanation actually survives.

hero_moments.label: A believable game becomes ridiculous
hero_moments.text: One prepared change turns a normal delivery or escape into a surprising crew problem; its consequence stays understandable.

hero_moments.label: The evidence pays off
hero_moments.text: Revisit two or three earlier clues after the reveal. The viewer gets the satisfaction of solving the same puzzle, not an unrelated backstage montage.

contingencies.label: Someone identifies it immediately
contingencies.text: Do not reset their knowledge or ask them to fake belief. Shift to whether Alex can convince the others, or whether the crew can find every planted change.

contingencies.label: Everyone believes too long
contingencies.text: Let the mission introduce a stronger, playable inconsistency. The reveal still needs evidence and a satisfying reaction; extra minutes of driving are not suspense.

contingencies.label: A target already knows
contingencies.text: Reframe their role openly in the planning/edit. The remaining unaware reactions can carry the prank without fabricated innocence.

contingencies.label: The build cannot support exploration
contingencies.text: Use a bounded route and a clear mission boundary. A convincing small experience is preferable to promising a whole unexplorable game.

packaging.label: Mystery access
packaging.text: Large photographic host holding one intriguing object beside a beautiful game scene. The object is a metaphor for access, not evidence of an actual leaked drive.

packaging.label: Is this real?
packaging.text: Real host at a station with one striking in-game vista or uncanny detail. Keep the uncertainty in the image and avoid an obvious prank reveal.

packaging.label: Title alignment
packaging.text: I Found The Leaked GTA 6 remains a working packaging test. The episode must reveal that it is staged; do not invent genuine developer access or unsupported provenance to justify the title.

production.label: Playable scope
production.text: Build one convincing district/route and three reliable mission interactions, with operator controls and reset points. More visual detail only helps if the crew can play it.

production.label: Source of the illusion
production.text: Visual polish, selected models and post effects support the story. Upscaling or AI-assisted development does not turn GTA 5 into actual GTA 6.

production.label: Reaction capture
production.text: Preserve each target’s first encounter, questions and the moment their belief changes. Later pickups should not be presented as first reactions.

production.label: Reveal proof
production.text: Capture a simple demonstration of the changes Alex controlled so the ending answers the audience’s questions.

post.label: Keep the audience guessing fairly
post.text: Withhold the explicit mechanism, but include real clues and doubts. Avoid editing a sincere objection out just to claim the crew was completely fooled.

post.label: Escalation
post.text: Move from plausible polish to a small oddity, then a consequential inconsistency, then the reveal. Each step changes what the crew does.

post.label: Pacing
post.text: Cut unproductive navigation and technical explanations. Keep the moments where a player tests, doubts, commits or catches Alex.

post.label: Ending
post.text: Resolve the prank, identify the custom experience and pay off the strongest clue. Let the final cast reaction close the story.

shorts.label: Suspicion without the answer
shorts.text: One strange interaction and a cast theory, with a clear route to the full episode after release.

shorts.label: Reveal extract
shorts.text: After the long-form reveal is public, show the clue, the explanation and the immediate reaction as a complete short.

shorts.label: Playable absurdity
shorts.text: A standalone mission change with its own funny consequence; it should still make sense without the leak premise.

success_checks: A non-gamer understands the mission and why the supposed access matters.
Suspicion produces new action instead of repetitive dialogue.
The reveal explains the planted clues and correctly identifies the build.
Claims about who knew the prank match the actual briefing and footage.
open_choices: Choose the bounded custom route and three prepared interactions after a playable test.
Confirm the cast knowledge boundary and what Alex can control live.
Choose the strongest reveal mechanism and a package that preserves uncertainty without inventing genuine leak evidence.

references.title: Prisoner Drive Thru Prank
references.observation: Observed source image: a real host in an orange prisoner costume inside a car, with a highlighted secondary face. The prank performance and human context are useful; the source is 2.94x.

references.title: 365 PRANKS IN 365 DAYS!!
references.observation: Original is a two-panel prank thumbnail. One panel places a threat behind an unaware person; our chase combines that relation into a single coherent game scene.

references.title: BUSTING VIRAL TIKTOK GADGETS!!
references.observation: Large host gesture at left presents one surprising gadget mechanism at right. We keep the presentation gesture and replace the dark background with the requested blue sky.

episodes.evidence_note: Public prank and gaming references support adjacent packaging/story analysis. They do not prove that a fake-GTA-access premise will outperform or that these specific reactions will occur.

episodes.title: I Survived 100 Hours in GTA
episodes.summary: Alex, Alan, Kat, Tanner and Shawn start separate GTA 6 runs in one room, and the first person to finish wins and lets the whole crew leave.
episodes.status: Actual GTA 6, five individual runs and first-finisher group release are confirmed; finish proof and competition rules below remain to agree.
episodes.viewer_promise: Five personalities race toward one clear finish while sharing the consequences of staying in the room. The audience can follow the leader, recoveries and crew dynamics without knowing GTA missions.
confirmed: Five players each have an individual game run; this is not assumed to be shared story co-op.
The first completion wins and releases everyone together.
100 hours is a working title. Actual elapsed duration determines the final truthful package.
Godzilla is in the first mashup video, not this completion challenge.
Record from actual game access, assemble while recording and publish ASAP after the winner, group release and final QC.
episodes.objective: Be the first to complete the agreed main-story finish condition in actual GTA 6.

rules.label: Matched start
rules.text: Begin from the same agreed game state and use the same difficulty/settings where the actual game allows them. Record the starts and any unavoidable difference.

rules.label: Finish proof
rules.text: Recommended: the agreed main-story ending/credits checkpoint, chosen after the real game’s completion routes are understood. Side activities and 100% completion are excluded unless the cast deliberately chooses a different premise.

rules.label: Individual runs
rules.text: Each player controls their own run. No save transfers, substitute players or unannounced skips. Agree any assistance policy before the race.

rules.label: Help policy proposal
rules.text: Players can talk and exchange advice because their shared exit encourages cooperation; nobody takes over another person’s controls. This creates a useful tension between personal victory and collective release.

rules.label: Failures and interruptions
rules.text: Normal in-game failures use the game’s normal retry/save system. Log a technical outage separately and apply the same agreed remedy to everyone; the precise remedy is a pending rule.

rules.label: Room and breaks
rules.text: Agree a fair rest/break policy before recording. Keep the elapsed clock honest and explain meaningful pauses. The room is the challenge setting; the premise does not depend on denying ordinary needs.

rules.label: Winner and release
rules.text: The first verified finish ends the competition and releases all five. There is no requirement to film the others completing separate endings after the race is over.

intro.label: 0 (First Frame)–5s
intro.text: Five occupied stations, the room door closing and a readable elapsed clock. Cut to a genuine late-race reaction that does not reveal who wins.

intro.label: 5s–15s
intro.text: “We can’t leave until one of us beats GTA 6.” Explain that everyone has their own run and the first finisher releases the entire crew. Show the agreed finish marker.

intro.label: 15s–30s
intro.text: Start the real competition. One player gains an early advantage while another faces a readable setback; establish the cast through choices and reactions, not a long setup tour.

story.action: Show matched starts, the room promise and five clear progress lanes. Use only the first meaningful mission decisions needed to understand each competitor.
story.question: Who gets ahead first?

story.action: Find the first genuine skill gap or mistake. Explain what the setback costs in progress, rather than assuming viewers know the mission.
story.question: Is the early leader actually the strongest player?

story.phase: The room becomes part of the story
story.action: Use breaks, food, rivalry and advice where they change the competition. Time jumps are explicitly labeled; do not confuse hours elapsed with hours of uninterrupted play.
story.question: Will they prioritize winning or helping someone finish?

story.action: Crosscut actual reversals and approaching finish checkpoints. A delayed feed or editing choice must not imply a close race that did not happen.
story.question: Can the trailing player catch the real leader?

story.action: Hold enough gameplay and reaction to establish the actual ending checkpoint. Confirm who finished first using synchronized records, then reveal the winner.
story.question: Is this the run that finally lets everyone out?

story.action: Show the whole crew leaving together and a concise final progress/elapsed-time wrap-up. Their unfinished runs are a scoreboard recap, not a new requirement to stay.
story.question: How long did it really take, and who was closest behind?

cast_roles.label: All five competitors
cast_roles.text: Alex, Alan, Kat, Tanner and Shawn each have a visible progress lane. Let the footage establish the confident starter, surprise leader, helper and comeback player; do not assign fictional skill rankings in advance.

cast_roles.label: Crew tension
cast_roles.text: Someone may help a rival because any winner lets them leave, then regret giving away their lead. Follow that tension only if it happens.

cast_roles.label: Winner uncertainty
cast_roles.text: Build the edit around actual progress and finish proof. Either twin or any crew member can carry the decisive final run.

hero_moments.label: A clear progress reversal
hero_moments.text: A player loses an apparent lead through a normal mission failure, while another completes a visible milestone. Explain both sides of the change.

hero_moments.label: Help the rival
hero_moments.text: Keep a real exchange where advice makes the group’s exit more likely but threatens the helper’s chance to win.

hero_moments.label: The finish in the room
hero_moments.text: Capture the winning game state, the winner’s first reaction, the others discovering it and the group-release action as one connected payoff.

contingencies.label: It takes far less than 100 hours
contingencies.text: Use the actual duration or a completion-led title. Do not prolong the recording or fabricate the clock to preserve a working headline.

contingencies.label: It takes much longer
contingencies.text: Follow the agreed break/save policy, keep the room story truthful and let recording length determine the edit; no fixed 100-hour quota is assumed.

contingencies.label: The winner leads comfortably
contingencies.text: Use the genuine suspense of whether they can finish and release the crew. Do not fabricate an opponent who is seconds behind.

contingencies.label: Two players appear to finish together
contingencies.text: Use synchronized game capture and the agreed checkpoint to resolve order. Establish a tie rule before recording rather than improvising a favorable winner.

contingencies.label: Actual GTA 6 access/capture is not proved
contingencies.text: Keep the episode pending. The modded GTA 5/recreation route belongs to the custom episodes and cannot be relabeled actual GTA 6.

packaging.label: Room and race
packaging.text: A photographic host in the foreground, the other four occupied stations and one clear door/clock cue. The image should communicate “finish the game to get out.”

packaging.label: Real elapsed time
packaging.text: A tired or triumphant real cast reaction beside a readable elapsed clock can work after the duration is known. Do not bake an unearned 100-hour claim into the final art.

packaging.label: Title tests
packaging.text: Keep I Survived 100 Hours in GTA as provisional. I Beat GTA 6 and a completion/room-led title are alternatives; choose after footage establishes the actual story.

production.label: Actual access and individual state
production.text: Prove five actual game runs, settings, save states and supported access/capture. PCs may be capture/control stations, but that is not proof of a native PC version.

production.label: Finish verification
production.text: Use synchronized timestamps on the game and room records. Preserve uninterrupted evidence around each possible winning checkpoint.

production.label: Long-session capture
production.text: Test storage rollover, recording continuity, game saves and a recovery procedure before relying on a long recording. Detailed infrastructure costs stay in the private packet.

production.label: Rolling post
production.text: Log milestone progress and assemble while recording. The final cut waits for verified winner/group release and final picture, sound and factual QC.

post.label: Readable progress
post.text: Use a five-lane scoreboard tied to actual verified milestones. Do not invent a percentage when the game supplies no reliable completion measure.

post.label: Compress repetition
post.text: Summarize repeated driving or failed attempts when they add no new decision; preserve the attempt that changes the lead or the player’s strategy.

post.label: Truthful time
post.text: Show elapsed-time jumps and meaningful breaks clearly. A tight edit can still make the length and changing room mood understandable.

post.label: ASAP publication
post.text: Prepare reusable progress graphics and ongoing assemblies, then finish from the real outcome. Fast turnaround does not justify losing the finish proof or confusing the release rule.

shorts.label: A comeback
shorts.text: One setback, the player’s changed approach and the result, with a simple progress graphic.

shorts.label: Crew rivalry

shorts.label: Everyone gets out
